text:
2 Question 3: filtering the DNS snapshot
The starter below loads the central \(128^3\) samples, applies the normalized box filter for one width at a time and forms the exact SGS stress \(\tau_{ij}=\overline{u_iu_j}-\bar u_i\bar u_j\) and the resolved strain rate \(\bar S_{ij}\). Everything after that (SGS energy, eigenvalues, energy transfer, the Smagorinsky comparison and the plots) is your analysis.
import numpy as np
from scipy.ndimage import uniform_filter

raw = np.load("/project/60004/03_Assignment4/isotropic/isotropic_256_t0001.npy", mmap_mode="r")
u = np.array(raw[64:192, 64:192, 64:192], dtype=np.float64)   # central 128^3 samples, shape (128, 128, 128, 3)
h = 2 * np.pi / 1024                                          # sampling spacing
core = (slice(10, -10),) * 3                                  # common interior used for every comparison

def box_filter(a, n):
    """Normalized n x n x n box filter on the original mesh. mode="nearest" pads instead of
    wrapping; the padded faces lie outside the common interior."""
    return uniform_filter(a, size=n, mode="nearest")

def filtered_fields(u, n):
    """Return the filtered velocity ub (..., 3), the SGS stress tau (..., 3, 3) and the resolved
    strain rate S (..., 3, 3) for a box filter of n samples per direction (Delta = n h)."""
    ub = np.stack([box_filter(u[..., i], n) for i in range(3)], axis=-1)
    tau = np.empty(u.shape[:3] + (3, 3))
    grad = np.empty_like(tau)
    for i in range(3):
        for j in range(3):
            tau[..., i, j] = box_filter(u[..., i] * u[..., j], n) - ub[..., i] * ub[..., j]
            grad[..., i, j] = np.gradient(ub[..., i], h, axis=j, edge_order=2)  # d(ub_i)/dx_j, centered inside
    S = 0.5 * (grad + np.swapaxes(grad, -1, -2))
    return ub, tau, S

for n in (5, 9, 17):
    ub, tau, S = filtered_fields(u, n)
    # Your analysis on the interior, e.g. with tau[core] and S[core].
    del ub, tau, S          # about 0.5 GB per width; free it before the next one
Work width by width as above rather than storing all three, and keep only the quantities you need (means, histograms, a plane for plotting).

title: Assignment 4: LES guide
section: 3 Question 4: the LES of the backward-facing step
text:
3 Question 4: the LES of the backward-facing step

3.1 What was simulated
The geometry and flow conditions are those of the step you studied in Assignment 3:







Quantity
Value




Step height and inlet-channel height
\(h = 0.1\,\mathrm{m}\) (expansion ratio 2)


Bulk velocity in the inlet channel
\(U_b = 2.0424\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)


Kinematic viscosity
\(\nu = 1.48\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\)


Reynolds number
\(Re = U_b h/\nu = 13\,800\) (nominal inflow \(Re_\tau = 395\) based on the channel half-height)


Reference data
DNS of [1], mean reattachment \(x_r/h = 8.8\)



The LES is three-dimensional and time-dependent. It resolves the large turbulent motions and models only the effect of the scales smaller than the grid. Fig. 1 shows how the domain is built.






Figure 1: Setup of the LES. A periodic precursor channel and the step domain belong to one mesh but are not connected; the step inlet copies its velocity from a sampling plane inside the precursor at every time step. Schematic, not to scale.





3.2 How the turbulent inflow is generated
An LES needs an inflow that is itself turbulent: realistic, time-dependent eddies with the right statistics. A steady profile, or a profile with random noise added, would take a long distance to develop into real turbulence, and that development would change the separation at the step. Common remedies are synthetic-turbulence generators, recycling methods and precursor simulations. This case uses an embedded precursor.

A periodic channel runs alongside the step. The block on the left of Fig. 1 is a channel of height \(h\) and length \(5h\). Its inlet and outlet patches are cyclic, so flow leaving it re-enters at its inlet and the turbulence recirculates indefinitely. Without a driving force, wall friction would slowly stop the flow. A meanVelocityForce source adds exactly the streamwise pressure gradient needed to keep the bulk velocity at \(U_b\):


system/fvOptions (excerpt)

momentumSource
{
    type            meanVelocityForce;
    selectionMode   cellSet;
    cellSet         precursor;      // only the precursor cells, created by topoSet
    fields          (U);
    Ubar            ($u_0 0 0);     // target bulk velocity Ub
}

The step inlet copies the precursor. The step inlet is a mappedPatch. At every time step it takes the velocity (and eddy viscosity) from the nearest cells on a plane shifted by a fixed offset into the middle of the precursor:


system/blockMeshDict (inlet patch)

inlet_bfs
{
    type            mappedPatch;
    sampleMode      nearestCell;    // values from the nearest cell ...
    offsetMode      uniform;
    offset          (#eval"$x_off+$l_pre/2+$l_inlet" 0 0);   // ... on a plane inside the precursor
    faces           ((4 7 3 0));
}

The velocity field uses the matching boundary condition type mapped; on this patch. The step therefore sees the precursor’s instantaneous turbulence, eddy by eddy.
The forcing needs a cell set. system/topoSetDict creates the cell set precursor from a box around the precursor block. In a parallel run, topoSet -parallel must run before the solver so that every processor knows its precursor cells.







NoteWhy a modified solver?



The precursor is fully periodic and has no outlet, so nothing fixes its pressure level: any constant can be added to \(p\) there without changing the flow. The step domain has a fixed-pressure outlet, so OpenFOAM does not apply a pressure reference, and the precursor level can drift. The run therefore used pimpleFoamPreRef, a copy of the standard pimpleFoam in which the pressure reference (pRefPoint in system/fvSolution) is always enforced. prepare_solver.py creates it from the installed source; nothing else in the solver changes.


Initial condition. The precursor started from a separate, wider periodic-channel LES, mapped onto the narrower span and rescaled to \(U_b\) (see mapping_report.json). The step region started from an earlier LES of the same geometry. Neither is a physical continuation, which is why the run first had an adjustment phase without statistics (see the run history).


3.3 The mesh
The mesh is made by blockMesh from system/blockMeshDict: block P for the precursor and blocks A to E for the step domain, with all parameters in globalVariables.

819 000 hexahedral cells in total, including 52 500 in the precursor.
Base cell size 5 mm (20 cells across \(h\) in the core flow), graded towards the walls (wall_grading 8).
25 cells across the span \(\pi h/2\); the span is periodic (cyclic front and back patches).

To judge the resolution, express the spacing in wall units, \(\Delta^+ = \Delta\,u_\tau/\nu\). For the inflow channel, \(Re_\tau = u_\tau\,(h/2)/\nu = 395\) gives \(u_\tau \approx 0.117\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and a viscous length \(\nu/u_\tau \approx 0.13\,\mathrm{mm}\). For example, the 5 mm core cells are about \(39\) wall units. Downstream of the step \(u_\tau\) varies strongly, and it is small inside the recirculation region, so local values differ; the yPlus history in LES_Q4/histories reports the logged first-cell values. Commonly quoted targets for wall-resolved LES of wall-bounded flows are roughly \(\Delta x^+ \approx 50\)–\(150\), \(\Delta z^+ \approx 15\)–\(40\) and a first cell at \(y^+ \lesssim 1\).


3.4 Subgrid model and numerics








Setting
Value
File




SGS model
Smagorinsky, filter width \(\Delta = V^{1/3}\) (cubeRootVol)
constant/turbulenceProperties


Wall treatment
no-slip velocity; zeroGradient \(\nu_t\) at the walls; no wall damping
boundary conditions in 50.1/U, 50.1/nut


Time integration
backward (second order), adaptive \(\Delta t\) with \(\mathrm{Co}_{\max}=0.5\), about \(2.2\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{s}\)
system/fvSchemes, system/controlDict


Pressure-velocity coupling
PIMPLE with 1 outer and 2 pressure correctors (PISO-like)
system/fvSolution


Convection
central differencing (Gauss linear)
system/fvSchemes


Safety limiter
limitVelocity at \(10\,U_b\)
system/fvOptions



OpenFOAM’s Smagorinsky constants. OpenFOAM writes the model with two constants. It estimates the subgrid energy from a local balance of production and dissipation, \(k_{\mathrm{sgs}} = (2C_k/C_e)\,\Delta^2\,\overline{S}_{ij}\overline{S}_{ij}\), and sets \(\nu_t = C_k\,\Delta\sqrt{k_{\mathrm{sgs}}}\). Comparing with the classical form \(\nu_t=(C_s\Delta)^2\sqrt{2\overline{S}_{ij}\overline{S}_{ij}}\) gives
\[
C_s = C_k^{3/4}\,C_e^{-1/4} = 0.094^{3/4}\times1.048^{-1/4} \approx 0.17,
\]
the same coefficient you tested a priori on filtered DNS in Question 3.
Why central differencing? In an LES the scheme acts on resolved eddies. Upwind-type schemes add numerical dissipation that damps the smallest resolved eddies and competes with the SGS model, as discussed in the LES lectures. Central schemes keep that dissipation low, so the SGS model, not the scheme, removes most of the energy at the grid scale.


3.5 What was recorded
The function objects in system/FOs/ produced the data in LES_Q4:

fieldAverage: running time averages UMean, pMean, nutMean, wallShearStressMean, yPlusMean, and the resolved covariance UPrime2Mean \(=\langle(\overline{u}_i-\langle\overline{u}_i\rangle)(\overline{u}_j-\langle\overline{u}_j\rangle)\rangle_t\), stored in the order xx xy xz yy yz zz. The supplied statistics cover \(t = 25\) to \(50.1\,\mathrm{s}\). With adaptive time steps, each sample is weighted by its time step.
Profiles (profile_*h.csv) are these time averages, additionally averaged over the periodic span.
Separate windows (blocks_*h.csv and the extra wall-shear columns) are obtained from the cumulative averages. If \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are the means from the common start to \(t_1\) and \(t_2\), accumulated over durations \(T_1\) and \(T_2\), the mean over \([t_1,t_2]\) is \((T_2M_2-T_1M_1)/(T_2-T_1)\). Subtracting the means directly would be wrong.
tauW writes the wall shear stress. OpenFOAM’s sign is negative for ordinary forward flow at the lower wall; the README gives the conversion to a conventional skin-friction coefficient.
probes record the velocity at four points every 10th time step (coordinates in the file header). fluxChecks (every 20th step), uBulk and yPlus (at every field write, once per second in the production run) and courantNumber monitor the run.
cutplanes wrote the \(z=0\) plane every \(0.01\,\mathrm{s}\). The data contain five widely separated planes (25 to 45 s) and a dense sequence of 101 planes from \(49\) to \(50\,\mathrm{s}\).

text:

text:
NoteWhat this assignment is about



This assignment ties together the two ways we characterise a turbulent flow, both on Johns Hopkins isotropic DNS data. First you measure the flow’s integral quantities directly from the field — the turbulent kinetic energy \(k\), the dissipation rate \(\varepsilon\), and the characteristic scales built from them — on a small full-resolution \(256^3\) ensemble (the small scales must be resolved for \(\varepsilon\)). Then you turn to the two-point correlation: you verify two classical isotropy results on a larger \(512^3\) periodic box (a fresh download that samples the large-scale correlations far better), reproducing the longitudinal and transverse autocorrelations \(f(r)\) and \(g(r)\) (the classic grid-turbulence measurement) and the integral length scales.

title: Assignment 2a: Turbulent kinetic energy and two-point correlations
text:
The turbulent kinetic energy equation
Applying the Reynolds decomposition \(u_i = \langle u_i\rangle + u_i'\) to the Navier–Stokes equations and taking the mean gives the transport equation for the turbulent kinetic energy \(k = \tfrac12\langle u_i' u_i'\rangle\):
\[
\underbrace{\frac{\partial k}{\partial t}}_{\text{unsteady}}
+ \underbrace{\langle u_j\rangle \frac{\partial k}{\partial x_j}}_{\text{advection}}
= \underbrace{-\langle u_i' u_j'\rangle \frac{\partial \langle u_i\rangle}{\partial x_j}}_{\text{production } \mathcal{P}}
- \underbrace{\varepsilon}_{\text{dissipation}}
+ \underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}\!\left(\cdots\right)}_{\text{transport } \mathcal{T}}
\tag{1}\]
with the dissipation rate
\[
\varepsilon = 2\nu \langle s_{ij}' s_{ij}'\rangle,
\qquad
s_{ij}' = \tfrac12\!\left(\frac{\partial u_i'}{\partial x_j} + \frac{\partial u_j'}{\partial x_i}\right).
\tag{2}\]






TipWhy the budget collapses for our flow



Forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence is the cleanest possible case for Eq. 1, because almost every term drops out:

No mean shear. \(\langle u_i\rangle \approx 0\) everywhere, so the mean advection term and the production term \(\mathcal{P} = -\langle u_i' u_j'\rangle\,\partial_j\langle u_i\rangle\) both vanish — there is no mean gradient to extract energy from.
Homogeneity. Statistics do not depend on position, so every spatial divergence — the transport term \(\mathcal{T}\) — averages to zero.
Stationarity. The forcing injects energy at the large scales at a mean rate \(\mathcal{F}\) that, on average, holds \(\partial k/\partial t = 0\).

What remains is a single statement: injection balances dissipation, \(\mathcal{F} = \varepsilon\). You cannot measure the artificial forcing \(\mathcal{F}\) from a snapshot, but you can measure \(k\) and \(\varepsilon\) directly — and from them every characteristic scale of the flow.

text:
Loading the cube
The budget tasks (1–4) use a small full-resolution \(256^3\) ensemble — five time-separated snapshots isotropic_256_t*.npy, each a \((256,256,256,3)\) array with the velocity components on the last axis (already axis-aligned). The grid spacing is that of the parent \(1024^3\) simulation, \(dx = 2\pi/1024\), so the small scales are resolved. A single \(256^3\) cube spans only about one integral scale, so average each quantity over the five snapshots — the independent realizations converge the large-scale statistics (\(k\), \(\mathrm{Re}_\lambda\)). Part (c) loads a separate, larger cube for the correlations.

    a = np.load(path).astype(np.float64)
    return [a[..., i] - a[..., i].mean() for i in range(3)]

text:
Task 2 — Turbulent kinetic energy






ImportantTask 2



Compute the turbulent kinetic energy
\[
k = \tfrac12\langle u_i' u_i'\rangle
  = \tfrac12\!\left(\langle u_1'^2\rangle + \langle u_2'^2\rangle + \langle u_3'^2\rangle\right).
\]
Report \(k\) and the equivalent single-component rms velocity \(u_{\mathrm{rms}} = \sqrt{2k/3}\).

title: Assignment 2a: Turbulent kinetic energy and two-point correlations
text:
Task 3 — Dissipation rate






ImportantTask 3



Evaluate the dissipation rate from its definition, Eq. 2. Use numpy.gradient with spacing dx to obtain the nine fluctuating velocity gradients \(\partial u_i'/\partial x_j\), build the fluctuating strain-rate tensor \(s_{ij}'\), and average:
\[
\varepsilon = 2\nu\,\langle s_{ij}' s_{ij}'\rangle .
\]
Then compute the isotropic surrogate \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{iso}} = 15\,\nu\,\big\langle (\partial u_1'/\partial x_1)^2\big\rangle\), which uses a single gradient, and compare the two. How close are they, and why should they agree for this flow?

text:
Task 4 — Characteristic scales






ImportantTask 4



From \(k\), \(\varepsilon\) and \(\nu\) alone, compute:

the Kolmogorov scales \(\eta = (\nu^3/\varepsilon)^{1/4}\), \(\tau_\eta = (\nu/\varepsilon)^{1/2}\), \(u_\eta = (\nu\varepsilon)^{1/4}\);
the Taylor microscale \(\lambda = \sqrt{10\,\nu k/\varepsilon}\);
the Taylor-microscale Reynolds number \(\mathrm{Re}_\lambda = \dfrac{u_{\mathrm{rms}}\,\lambda}{\nu} = \sqrt{\dfrac{20\,k^2}{3\,\nu\,\varepsilon}}\).

Report your measured \(\mathrm{Re}_\lambda\). (A single \(256^3\) cube is only \(\sim\)one integral scale wide, so averaging the five time-separated snapshots is what converges \(k\) and \(\mathrm{Re}_\lambda\) toward the \(433\) of the full dataset.)

title: Assignment 2a: Turbulent kinetic energy and two-point correlations
text:
Background
For homogeneous isotropic turbulence the two-point correlation \[
R_{ij}(\mathbf r)=\langle u_i'(\mathbf x+\mathbf r)\,u_j'(\mathbf x)\rangle
\] is completely determined by two scalar functions of the separation distance — the longitudinal and transverse autocorrelations, \[
f(r)=\frac{\langle u_1'(\mathbf x+r\mathbf e_1)\,u_1'(\mathbf x)\rangle}{\langle u_1'^2\rangle},
\qquad
g(r)=\frac{\langle u_2'(\mathbf x+r\mathbf e_1)\,u_2'(\mathbf x)\rangle}{\langle u_2'^2\rangle},
\] with \(f(0)=g(0)=1\). Continuity (\(\partial R_{ij}/\partial r_j=0\)) links the two: \[
g(r)=f(r)+\tfrac12\,r\,\frac{\partial f}{\partial r}. \tag{$\star$}
\] The integral length scales are the areas under the curves, \[
L_{11}=\int_0^\infty f(r)\,dr,\qquad L_{22}=\int_0^\infty g(r)\,dr .
\]
Two classical consequences of \((\star)\), which you will verify on the data below, are that the transverse integral scale is half the longitudinal one, \(L_{22}=\tfrac12 L_{11}\), and that the transverse correlation has zero first moment, \(\int_0^\infty r\,g\,dr=0\) — so \(g\) must dip negative at intermediate \(r\).
Now measure \(f\), \(g\) and the length scales on the real cube and check both. Because HIT has no mean flow, the fluctuations are the whole signal (\(u_i'\approx u_i\)).

title: Assignment 2a: Turbulent kinetic energy and two-point correlations
text:
c.2 An autocorrelation helper (FFT)
The two-point correlation along one axis is an autocorrelation, so the FFT (Wiener–Khinchin theorem) computes it in one shot; average over the two perpendicular directions to reduce the noise:

def corr_axis(field, axis):
    """Normalized autocorrelation of `field` along `axis`, averaged over the plane."""
    F = np.fft.fft(field, axis=axis)
    R = np.fft.ifft((F*np.conj(F)).real, axis=axis).real        # Wiener–Khinchin
    R = R.mean(axis=tuple(k for k in range(3) if k != axis))    # average other two axes
    return R[:field.shape[axis]//2] / R[0]                      # nonneg lags, R(0)=1

title: Slurm
text:
1 The batch script
The script states the resources you need (walltime, cores, memory) in #SBATCH lines, then runs your commands:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=<account>     # your course allocation (shown after you log in)
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00         # walltime HH:MM:SS — the job is killed after this
#SBATCH --ntasks=4              # number of parallel tasks (e.g. MPI ranks)
#SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=2G        # memory per task

module load openfoam/v2412
srun myParallelCommand          # Slurm launches the tasks across the requested cores

title: Slurm
text:
2 An OpenFOAM batch job
A real parallel OpenFOAM run follows the decompose → solve → reconstruct pattern from the Running in parallel page, wrapped in one script. Save this as job.sh inside your case folder:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=<account>     # your course allocation
#SBATCH --job-name=channel395   # a name you will recognise in the queue
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00         # walltime HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --ntasks=8              # 8 MPI ranks  ==  8 subdomains
#SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=2G        # memory per rank
#SBATCH --output=%x-%j.out      # log file named <job-name>-<jobid>.out

module load openfoam/v2412      # make the OpenFOAM commands available

decomposePar -force             # split the case into processor0/ ... processor7/
srun simpleFoam -parallel       # run the solver across the 8 ranks
reconstructPar -latestTime      # merge the final result back into one case






ImportantKeep --ntasks and numberOfSubdomains in step



The --ntasks=8 here must equal numberOfSubdomains in system/decomposeParDict (and hence the number of processor* folders). If they disagree, the parallel run aborts immediately. Change one, change the other.

title: Slurm
section: 3 Submitting your job, step by step
text:
3 Submitting your job, step by step

Get the case onto the cluster and cd into it (see Get the case on the cluster).
Mesh and check on the login node first. blockMesh / snappyHexMesh and checkMesh are cheap — run them interactively so you never waste a queued job on a broken mesh.
Match the counts. Set numberOfSubdomains in system/decomposeParDict equal to the --ntasks in job.sh.
Edit job.sh — set --account, a realistic --time, and --ntasks.
Submit it: sbatch job.sh. Slurm prints a job id and places the job in the queue.
Watch it with squeue -u $USER; once it starts, the solver output streams to the channel395-<jobid>.out log named by --output.
Collect the result. reconstructPar has already merged the final time, so copy the case back (or open it directly in ParaView) when the job finishes.

3 Connecting over SSH (advanced)






NoteFor later



You do not need this for the course: the JupyterLab terminal above is enough. Once command-line access is introduced, you can connect from a terminal on your own machine (macOS/Linux Terminal, or Windows PowerShell / WSL).



3.1 With a password
The simplest way is to log in with the username and password you created during Registration (replace <username> with your cluster username):
ssh <username>@mech501.calculquebec.cloud   # asks for your password each time


3.2 With an SSH key
An SSH key is a pair of files: a private key that never leaves your computer and a matching public key you place on the cluster. The server checks that the two match instead of asking for a password — so you log in without typing one, and it is more secure. Create a key once and copy the public half to the cluster:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519                              # creates ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (+ .pub)
ssh-copy-id <username>@mech501.calculquebec.cloud  # installs the public key there
From then on the same command logs you straight in, with no password:
ssh <username>@mech501.calculquebec.cloud


3.3 A shortcut: ~/.ssh/config
Save the connection details under a short name in ~/.ssh/config, so you can just type ssh turb:


~/.ssh/config

Host turb
    HostName mech501.calculquebec.cloud
    User <username>
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

ssh turb        # uses the HostName, User and key from the block above
Everything above — navigation, viewing files, vim, and the ~/.bashrc / ~/.vimrc setup — works exactly the same over SSH.

title: Assignment 3: OpenFOAM guide
text:
NoteWhat you will do



This guide supports Question 3 of the assignment PDF. Compare three configurations using developed channel inlets: standard \(k\)–\(\varepsilon\) with wall functions, wall-resolved SST, and SST with wall functions. Prepared inlet data are included; you do not need to run a precursor. No grid-convergence study is required. The PDF defines the assessed deliverables. Use at most four CPU cores in total for this exercise, including concurrent jobs.

title: Assignment 3: OpenFOAM guide
text:
1 Why study the backward-facing step?
At the step edge, the flow separates and forms a recirculation region before reattaching to the downstream wall. This simple geometry provides a demanding test of turbulence models: turbulent momentum transport affects the growth of the separated shear layer, the reattachment location and the recovery downstream. Comparing the three configurations with DNS helps us assess model and wall-treatment effects, and distinguish numerical convergence from physical accuracy.






Figure 1: Setup of the backward-facing-step calculation. The instructor supplies developed inlet profiles from a separate periodic channel precursor. The sketch is schematic, not to scale; the reattachment location is an output of the calculation.

title: Assignment 3: OpenFOAM guide
text:
2 Why supply a precursor profile?
The flow should reach the step with developed turbulent channel profiles. A precursor is a separate periodic channel calculation: flow leaving one end re-enters at the other, while a driving force balances wall friction and maintains the prescribed bulk velocity. It supplies the mean velocity and turbulence quantities at the step-case inlet. A uniform inlet would instead create a developing flow upstream and could change the separation and reattachment predictions.
For this assignment, the instructor has run one wall-resolved SST precursor and supplied its profiles for all three cases, sampled on each inlet mesh. These are steady RANS mean and turbulence-model fields, not instantaneous turbulent fluctuations. You do not run, sample or map a precursor. Start with the supplied step cases; their inlet data are already installed.






TipBefore running: parallel processing and Slurm




OpenFOAM: running in parallel explains decomposition, the parallel solver and reconstruction.
Slurm: requesting compute resources and monitoring jobs explains the scheduler and job management.

For this assignment, follow the manual run commands below inside an allocated compute session. No case-running bash helper script is required. The general guides also show batch scripts and eight-core examples; this assignment uses at most four cores in total, including concurrent runs. Match the allocated task count, numberOfSubdomains and MPI process count, and do not run the solver on the login node.

4 Prepare the wall treatment before running
The student cases leave k, nut and epsilon/omega wall conditions as explicit placeholders. Complete them consistently with each requested wall treatment.
For the two wall-function configurations, use a consistent wall-function approach and document its limitations in separated flow. The following wall entries are a starting configuration:

For example, the wall-patch regex entry in 0/nut becomes:
"(upstreamWall|stepWall|downstreamWall|upperWall)"
{
    type    nutkWallFunction;
    value   uniform 0;
}
Use value $internalField; for the initialization value of the corresponding k, epsilon or omega wall-function entries. Keep front/back patches empty and the mesh one cell thick in that direction. Apply the changes to your step cases only. The supplied template uses 0/ directly; it has no reset script to restore these edits.
Check actual \(y^+\) after solving. In attached regions a log-layer wall-function mesh should generally place the first cell outside the buffer layer; \(y^+\gtrsim30\) is a practical starting check, not a universal validity guarantee. Near separation and reattachment, a small reported wall-distance measure alone does not prove that the boundary layer is resolved. Report distributions and first-cell distances, not only a domain average.
The definition used by the diagnostic matters. With its default useWallFunction true, OpenFOAM’s yPlus uses the selected nut wall function’s expression where available. For nutkWallFunction, this is \(y^*=C_\mu^{1/4}\sqrt{k_P}\,y_P/\nu\), which need not equal the shear-based \(y^+=\sqrt{|\tau_w|/\rho}\,y_P/\nu\) away from equilibrium. For the resolved case’s fixed-zero wall nut, the diagnostic computes the flow-based value. Retain the supplied diagnostic settings and identify this distinction in your interpretation; a vanishing wall shear need not make the wall-function diagnostic vanish. See the OpenFOAM yPlus options.
The 02_SST_wallResolved/step configuration resolves the near-wall SST solution. Its supplied mesh targets first-cell \(y^+\lesssim1\) and enough smoothly graded cells through the boundary layer. Use fixedValue with value uniform 0; for wall k and nut, together with omegaWallFunction for wall omega and noSlip for velocity. At this resolution the omega boundary treatment supplies its viscous near-wall behavior; the presence of “WallFunction” in that boundary-condition name does not make this a high-Re log-law calculation. Check the actual wall distance and solved \(y^+\).
Use the inlet dataset already included in each case. All datasets come from one common continuous profile, sampled at the corresponding inlet face centres. Compare the SST cases as complete wall-treatment-and-mesh configurations, not as a pure boundary-condition switch on identical meshes. See the official wall-function overview, kqRWallFunction and nutkWallFunction documentation. Inspect the corresponding installed v2412 examples when editing the dictionaries.

title: Assignment 3: OpenFOAM guide
text:
8 Establish convergence and locate reattachment
Stop at the supplied cap of 10,000 SIMPLE iterations, or earlier if the stopping criteria are met. No extension beyond this cap is required. Keep residual histories for U, p, k and epsilon/omega, inspect continuity errors, and monitor inlet/outlet flux balance and reattachment over successive saved iterations. If the cap is reached, quantify remaining profile and reattachment changes and distinguish a sufficiently settled comparison from full convergence. A linear solver tolerance controls each equation solve; SIMPLE/residualControl controls stopping across outer iterations. Neither proves that the engineering quantities have stopped changing.
Inspect the stopping thresholds in SIMPLE/residualControl and report actual convergence and stabilization rather than relying on residual thresholds alone. Persistent oscillations should be reported; a steady solver does not automatically represent an unsteady physical mean accurately.

8.1 Worked example: reading a solver log
The following is the final iteration of the instructor’s standard \(k\)–\(\varepsilon\) wall-function run. Your iteration count and timings may differ. Read it in two stages: first the equation solves, then the checks on the resulting flow.

8.1.1 Initial and final residuals: two levels of iteration
For a discretized equation written as \(A\phi=b\), the algebraic residual is \(r=b-A\phi\). OpenFOAM reports a normalized measure of this imbalance. It is dimensionless, not an error in velocity or pressure units and not a percentage error relative to DNS.

Initial residual: the imbalance before this particular linear equation solve, using the current field estimate. “Initial” does not mean the beginning of the simulation.
Final residual: the imbalance after the inner linear solver has updated that field, with the current equation coefficients.
No Iterations: the number of inner solver iterations for this solve, not the number of SIMPLE iterations.

SIMPLE repeatedly updates the coupled velocity, pressure and turbulence equations. A small final residual shows that one current linear system has been solved accurately; the next outer iteration changes the coupled equations again. Follow the initial residual histories to assess progress of this outer iteration. Normalization is field- and state-dependent, so avoid interpreting residual ratios between different fields as ratios of physical errors. See the official residual definition.

ImportantWhich residual determines coupled convergence?



The initial residuals of all monitored equations determine whether the coupled SIMPLE iteration satisfies the prescribed convergence criteria. In this case, SIMPLE/residualControl checks the initial residuals for velocity, pressure and the turbulence quantities against their respective thresholds.
Why the initial residual? It measures the equation imbalance before another inner solve, after updates to the coupled fields. When these initial imbalances are sufficiently small across all monitored equations, the fields satisfy the coupled iteration’s stopping criteria to the chosen tolerances. A small final residual only shows that the current individual linear equation has been solved accurately.
Continue to check mass balance and stabilization of profiles and reattachment: satisfying the residual criteria is a numerical stopping test, not a guarantee of physical accuracy.

Reaching the iteration cap is also a possible exit and should be checked. See OpenFOAM solution controls.

Thus its final residual can be slightly above \(10^{-10}\) and still satisfy relTol. The three-iteration minimum also explains why an already very small pressure residual can undergo three more iterations.
The outer SIMPLE/residualControl thresholds are different: \(10^{-5}\) for p, \(10^{-6}\) for U, and \(10^{-6}\) for k and epsilon/omega. These monitor the initial equation residuals; for velocity, the largest solved component matters. At iteration 1544, Uy was \(1.0017\times10^{-6}\), just above its threshold. At 1545 it is \(9.9290\times10^{-7}\), just below it, and all monitored fields satisfy their thresholds. See SIMPLE case termination.

NoteAbout this page



This tutorial is a checklist, not a lecture. Everything here should be familiar from your fluid mechanics and math courses — we will briefly repeat some of it inside later exercises, but not re-teach it. title: Tutorial 0: Prerequisites
text:
1 Basic tensor algebra

1.1 What is a tensor?
A tensor is a physical quantity that exists independently of the coordinate system used to describe it — only its components change when the coordinate axes are rotated, and they do so in a well-defined way. Tensors are classified by their order (or rank), which is simply the number of indices needed to identify one component:

Order 0 — scalar (1 component): temperature \(T\), pressure \(p\), density \(\rho\).
Order 1 — vector (3 components): velocity \(u_i\), i.e. \((u_1, u_2, u_3)\).
Order 2 (9 components): stress \(\sigma_{ij}\), velocity gradient \(\partial u_i / \partial x_j\).

A second-order tensor is more than a matrix of numbers: it is a linear map between vectors. The classic example is the Cauchy stress tensor, which maps the unit normal \(n_j\) of a surface to the traction (force per area) \(t_i\) acting on it:
\[
t_i = \sigma_{ij}\, n_j
\tag{1}\]
We write tensors either in symbolic (bold) notation (\(\mathbf{u}\), \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\)) or in index notation (\(u_i\), \(\sigma_{ij}\)); Section 3 explains the index rules in detail.


1.2 Elementary operations
The operations you should recognize (in both notations):
\[
\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = a_i b_i, \qquad
(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{b})_i = A_{ij} b_j, \qquad
\mathbf{A} : \mathbf{B} = A_{ij} B_{ij}
\tag{2}\]
i.e. the dot product (two vectors → scalar), the tensor–vector product (→ vector, as in Eq. 1), and the double contraction (two tensors → scalar, used later for the dissipation rate).


1.3 Two special tensors: \(\delta_{ij}\) and \(\varepsilon_{ijk}\)
The Kronecker delta is the index form of the identity:
\[
\delta_{ij} =
\begin{cases}
1 & i = j \\
0 & i \neq j
\end{cases}
\tag{3}\]
Its key use is index substitution: multiplying by \(\delta_{ij}\) and summing renames an index, \(\delta_{ij}\, a_j = a_i\).
The Levi-Civita (permutation) symbol \(\varepsilon_{ijk}\) is the third-order companion of Eq. 3:
\[
\varepsilon_{ijk} =
\begin{cases}
+1 & (i,j,k) \text{ an even permutation of } (1,2,3)\text{: } 123,\, 231,\, 312 \\
-1 & (i,j,k) \text{ an odd permutation: } 132,\, 213,\, 321 \\
0 & \text{any index repeated}
\end{cases}
\tag{4}\]
It encodes cross products and hence rotation. The two expressions you will meet in this course are the cross product and the vorticity:
\[
(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})_i = \varepsilon_{ijk}\, a_j b_k,
\qquad
\omega_i = \varepsilon_{ijk} \frac{\partial u_k}{\partial x_j}
\tag{5}\]
Finally, the \(\varepsilon\)–\(\delta\) identity connects the two symbols and is the workhorse for simplifying double cross products:
\[
\varepsilon_{ijk}\, \varepsilon_{ilm} = \delta_{jl}\, \delta_{km} - \delta_{jm}\, \delta_{kl}
\tag{6}\]


1.4 Symmetric / antisymmetric decomposition
Any second-order tensor splits uniquely into a symmetric and an antisymmetric part:
\[
A_{ij} = \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2}(A_{ij} + A_{ji})}_{\text{symmetric}}
       + \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2}(A_{ij} - A_{ji})}_{\text{antisymmetric}}
\tag{7}\]
Applied to the velocity gradient this defines the strain-rate tensor \(S_{ij}\) (deformation) and the rotation-rate tensor \(\Omega_{ij}\) (rigid-body rotation, related to \(\omega_i\) from Eq. 5):
\[
\frac{\partial u_i}{\partial x_j} = S_{ij} + \Omega_{ij}, \qquad
S_{ij} = \frac{1}{2}\!\left(\frac{\partial u_i}{\partial x_j} + \frac{\partial u_j}{\partial x_i}\right), \qquad
\Omega_{ij} = \frac{1}{2}\!\left(\frac{\partial u_i}{\partial x_j} - \frac{\partial u_j}{\partial x_i}\right)
\tag{8}\]
This decomposition appears in essentially every turbulence model.






TipSelf-check — tensor algebra




What is \(\delta_{ii}\)? (Careful: repeated index!)
What are \(\varepsilon_{123}\), \(\varepsilon_{321}\), and \(\varepsilon_{112}\)?
Use Eq. 5 to show \(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{0}\).







NoteAnswers






\(\delta_{ii} = \delta_{11}+\delta_{22}+\delta_{33} = 3\).
\(\varepsilon_{123} = +1\), \(\varepsilon_{321} = -1\), \(\varepsilon_{112} = 0\).
\(\varepsilon_{ijk} a_j a_k = 0\) because \(a_j a_k\) is symmetric in \((j,k)\) while \(\varepsilon_{ijk}\) is antisymmetric — swapping \(j \leftrightarrow k\) flips the sign of the sum, so it must vanish.

2 Continuity and Navier–Stokes
For an incompressible, Newtonian fluid with constant properties, the governing variables and their SI units are:








Symbol
Quantity
SI units




\(u_i\)
velocity
\(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)


\(p\)
pressure
\(\mathrm{Pa} = \mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\)


\(\rho\)
density
\(\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\)


\(\mu\)
dynamic viscosity
\(\mathrm{Pa\,s} = \mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}\)


\(\nu = \mu/\rho\)
kinematic viscosity
\(\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\)



Continuity (conservation of mass) states that the velocity field is divergence-free; every term has units \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\):
\[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0
\qquad \left[\mathrm{s^{-1}}\right]
\tag{9}\]
Momentum (Navier–Stokes) is Newton’s second law per unit mass; every term has units of acceleration, \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\):
\[
\underbrace{\frac{\partial \mathbf{u}}{\partial t}}_{\text{unsteady}}
+ \underbrace{(\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla)\,\mathbf{u}}_{\text{convection}}
= \underbrace{-\frac{1}{\rho} \nabla p}_{\text{pressure gradient}}
+ \underbrace{\nu \nabla^2 \mathbf{u}}_{\text{viscous diffusion}}
\qquad \left[\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\right]
\tag{10}\]
Check the units term by term: \(\partial \mathbf{u}/\partial t \sim
\mathrm{(m/s)/s}\); convection \(\sim \mathrm{(m/s) \cdot (m/s)/m}\); pressure gradient \(\sim \mathrm{(Pa/m)/(kg/m^3)} =
\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-2} \cdot m^3\,kg^{-1}}\); viscous term \(\sim
\mathrm{(m^2/s) \cdot (m/s)/m^2}\) — all \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). ✓
Two things to remember: the convective term is the only nonlinear term — it is the reason turbulence exists and the reason the averaged equations don’t close — and pressure in incompressible flow is not a thermodynamic variable but a Lagrange multiplier that enforces Eq. 9.






TipSelf-check — governing equations



(The index-notation tools for 1 and 2 are introduced in Section 3 — come back here if needed.)

Using continuity (Eq. 9), show that the convective term can be written in conservative form: \(u_j\, \partial u_i / \partial x_j = \partial (u_i u_j) / \partial x_j\).
Take the divergence of Eq. 10 and use continuity to show that pressure satisfies a Poisson equation, \(\frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial^2 p}{\partial x_i \partial x_i}
= -\frac{\partial u_j}{\partial x_i} \frac{\partial u_i}{\partial x_j}\). What does this tell you about the role of pressure in incompressible flow?
The viscous dissipation rate per unit mass is \(\varepsilon = 2 \nu S_{ij} S_{ij}\) (with \(S_{ij}\) from Eq. 8). Show that its units are \(\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-3}} = \mathrm{W\,kg^{-1}}\).







NoteAnswers






Product rule: \(\partial (u_i u_j)/\partial x_j
= u_j\, \partial u_i/\partial x_j + u_i\, \underbrace{\partial u_j / \partial x_j}_{=\,0}\) — the last term vanishes by continuity. The conservative form is what finite-volume codes like OpenFOAM actually discretize.
Applying \(\partial/\partial x_i\) to each term: the unsteady term gives \(\partial(\partial u_i/\partial x_i)/\partial t = 0\) and the viscous term gives \(\nu\, \partial^2 (\partial u_i / \partial x_i)/\partial x_j \partial x_j = 0\) (both by continuity); the convective term leaves \(\partial u_j/\partial x_i\; \partial u_i/\partial x_j\). Hence the Poisson equation. Pressure has no evolution equation of its own: it is determined instantaneously by the velocity field (elliptic problem) and acts as a Lagrange multiplier that enforces Eq. 9 — this is why incompressible solvers need a pressure-correction step (e.g. PISO/SIMPLE in OpenFOAM).
\([\nu] = \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\) and \([S_{ij}] = \mathrm{s^{-1}}\), so \([\varepsilon] = \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}} \cdot \mathrm{s^{-2}}
= \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-3}}\). Since \(\mathrm{W\,kg^{-1}} = \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}\,kg^{-1}}
= \mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}} \cdot \mathrm{s^{-1}\,kg^{-1}}
= \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-3}}\), dissipation is a power per unit mass — kinetic energy converted to heat.

text:
3 Index notation
We will write most turbulence equations in Cartesian index (Einstein) notation. The rules:

A repeated (dummy) index in a term implies summation over 1–3: \(a_i b_i = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_3\).
A free index (appearing once) must match in every term of an equation and denotes three equations at once.
No index may appear more than twice in a single term.


3.1 Worked example 1: divergence of a vector
With the shorthand \(\partial/\partial x_j\), the divergence \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}\) has one repeated index \(j\) — so it is a scalar, written out as:
\[
\frac{\partial u_j}{\partial x_j}
= \frac{\partial u_1}{\partial x_1}
+ \frac{\partial u_2}{\partial x_2}
+ \frac{\partial u_3}{\partial x_3}
\tag{11}\]


3.2 Worked example 2: tensor–vector product
\(b_i = A_{ij}\, x_j\) has free index \(i\) and dummy index \(j\): it is three equations, each a sum of three terms. The first one (\(i = 1\)) reads
\[
b_1 = A_{11} x_1 + A_{12} x_2 + A_{13} x_3,
\tag{12}\]
and analogously for \(b_2\), \(b_3\) — exactly a matrix–vector product.


3.3 Navier–Stokes in index notation
Applying the same rules to Eq. 9 and Eq. 10:
\[
\frac{\partial u_j}{\partial x_j} = 0
\tag{13}\]
\[
\frac{\partial u_i}{\partial t}
+ u_j \frac{\partial u_i}{\partial x_j}
= -\frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial p}{\partial x_i}
+ \nu \frac{\partial^2 u_i}{\partial x_j \partial x_j}
\tag{14}\]
Compare with Eq. 11 and Eq. 12: continuity is a divergence (one dummy index, scalar equation), while in Eq. 14 the free index \(i\) says “one equation per velocity component” and the dummy index \(j\) sums the convective and viscous contributions from all three directions. You should be able to translate between Eq. 10 and Eq. 14 fluently — Reynolds averaging in the lectures happens almost entirely in index notation.






TipSelf-check — index notation




Write out the \(i = 2\) component of the convective term \(u_j\, \partial u_i / \partial x_j\).
Is that term linear in \(\mathbf{u}\)?
Is \(c_i = a_j b_j d_i\) valid index notation? What about \(c_i = a_j b_j d_j\)?







NoteAnswers






\(u_1 \frac{\partial u_2}{\partial x_1} + u_2 \frac{\partial u_2}{\partial x_2} + u_3 \frac{\partial u_2}{\partial x_3}\).
No — velocity multiplies its own gradient (quadratic). This term generates the Reynolds stresses under averaging.
Valid (\(j\) dummy, \(i\) free); invalid — \(j\) appears three times in one term.

Consider fully developed flow through a pipe (Fig. 1): we ask how the pressure drop \(\Delta p\) over a length \(L\) depends on the flow and fluid parameters.

The physical relationship is
\[
\Delta p = f(\rho,\ \mu,\ U,\ D,\ L),
\tag{15}\]
with dimensions (using \(\mathrm{M}\) = mass, \(\mathrm{L}\) = length, \(\mathrm{T}\) = time):

\(U\)
\(D\)
\(L\)




Dimensions

\(\mathrm{L}\)



Step 1 — count. \(n = 6\) variables, \(k = 3\) independent dimensions (\(\mathrm{M}, \mathrm{L}, \mathrm{T}\)) ⟹ the Buckingham-\(\Pi\) theorem guarantees \(n - k = 3\) independent dimensionless groups.
Step 2 — choose repeating variables. Pick \(k = 3\) variables that (i) together contain all three dimensions, (ii) are dimensionally independent of each other, and (iii) do not include the dependent variable \(\Delta p\). The standard choice is \(\rho\) (mass), \(U\) (time), \(D\) (length).
Step 3 — form the groups. Each remaining variable, multiplied by powers of the repeating ones, must come out dimensionless. For \(\mu\):
\[
\Pi_2 = \mu\, \rho^{a} U^{b} D^{c}
\;\;\Rightarrow\;\;
\mathrm{M}^{1+a}\ \mathrm{L}^{-1-3a+b+c}\ \mathrm{T}^{-1-b} \overset{!}{=} \mathrm{M}^0 \mathrm{L}^0 \mathrm{T}^0
\tag{16}\]
Setting each exponent to zero: \(\mathrm{M}\!: a = -1\); \(\mathrm{T}\!: b = -1\); then \(\mathrm{L}\!: c = -1\). Hence
\[
\Pi_2 = \frac{\mu}{\rho U D}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\Pi_2^{-1} = \frac{\rho U D}{\mu} = \mathrm{Re}.
\tag{17}\]
The same procedure applied to \(\Delta p\) and \(L\) gives the other two groups (do it yourself — self-check below):
\[
\Pi_1 = \frac{\Delta p}{\rho U^2}, \qquad
\Pi_3 = \frac{L}{D},
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
\frac{\Delta p}{\rho U^2} = \phi\!\left(\mathrm{Re},\ \frac{L}{D}\right)
\tag{18}\]
— six dimensional variables collapse to a relation between three numbers. That is exactly why friction-factor charts (Moody diagram) work.
The physical meaning of \(\mathrm{Re}\) is the ratio of inertial to viscous effects:
\[
\mathrm{Re} = \frac{\rho U D}{\mu} = \frac{U D}{\nu}
\sim \frac{\text{inertial forces}}{\text{viscous forces}}
\tag{19}\]
The same conclusion follows from non-dimensionalizing Eq. 14 with \(x_i^* = x_i / D\), \(u_i^* = u_i / U\), \(t^* = tU/D\), \(p^* = p / (\rho U^2)\):
\[
\frac{\partial u_i^*}{\partial t^*}
+ u_j^* \frac{\partial u_i^*}{\partial x_j^*}
= -\frac{\partial p^*}{\partial x_i^*}
+ \frac{1}{\mathrm{Re}} \frac{\partial^2 u_i^*}{\partial x_j^* \partial x_j^*}
\tag{20}\]
\(\mathrm{Re}\) is the only parameter left — two incompressible flows with the same geometry and Reynolds number are dynamically similar, and the viscous term becomes small (in a subtle, near-wall-dominated way) as \(\mathrm{Re} \to \infty\). This is the starting point of the course.






TipSelf-check — dimensional analysis




Derive \(\Pi_1\) in Eq. 18 by repeating Step 3 for \(\Delta p\).

Water flows at \(U = 1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) through a \(D = 5\,\mathrm{cm}\) pipe (\(\nu = 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\)). Compute \(\mathrm{Re}\). Laminar or turbulent?







NoteAnswers






\(\Delta p\, \rho^a U^b D^c\): \(\mathrm{M}\!: a=-1\); \(\mathrm{T}\!: b=-2\); \(\mathrm{L}\!: -1+3-2+c=0 \Rightarrow c=0\) — giving \(\Delta p / (\rho U^2)\).
The relative roughness \(k_s / D\) (the third parameter of the Moody diagram).

title: Tutorial 3: Turbulent channel flow
text:
NoteWhat this tutorial is about



In Tutorial 1, we studied turbulence without walls or mean shear. Here we introduce a canonical wall-bounded flow: a turbulent channel. We will explain how the flow is driven, where the turbulence gets its energy, and how instantaneous velocity fields become the profiles used in Assignment 3. Allow about 15 minutes. This page provides background; the assignment contains the assessed questions.

title: Tutorial 3: Turbulent channel flow
text:
1 Why a channel?
Consider two stationary parallel walls separated by \(2\delta\). Let \(x=x_1\) be streamwise, \(y=x_2\) the distance from the lower wall, and \(z=x_3\) spanwise. The lower wall is at \(y=0\) and the centerline at \(y=\delta\).






Figure 1: Channel geometry and a representative mean velocity profile. The computational domain repeats in the streamwise and spanwise directions.



The geometry is simple, but the turbulence is not. Instantaneous velocity varies in all three directions and in time. Once the flow is statistically stationary and fully developed, its mean statistics depend only on \(y\). This gives us a manageable setting for studying wall effects, shear production, unequal component energies and Reynolds-number dependence.
It also gives us exact mean-flow balances against which to check data and models. Channel DNS is consequently a useful benchmark, although success here does not establish accuracy for separated flows or complex geometries.






Figure 2: Channel-flow visualization used in the introductory lecture. Source: Nils Mueller, bachelor thesis, TU Darmstadt.

title: Tutorial 3: Turbulent channel flow
section: 2 How is turbulence generated and sustained?
text:
2 How is turbulence generated and sustained?
A pressure drop drives the mean flow. No-slip walls impose zero velocity at the surfaces, producing a mean velocity gradient. Disturbances can develop into turbulence at a suitable Reynolds number; in computations we commonly start from a turbulent restart or a mean profile with finite disturbances. A perfectly undisturbed laminar initialization should not be expected to become turbulent automatically.
Near a wall, wall-normal motion carries fluid between regions of different mean streamwise velocity. An ejection carries relatively slow fluid away from the lower wall (\(u'<0\), \(v'>0\)); a sweep brings relatively fast fluid toward it (\(u'>0\), \(v'<0\)). Both contribute negatively to \(\langle u'v'\rangle\). Streamwise streaks and vortical motions participate in the continuing regeneration of these fluctuations.
For the lower half-channel, the transfer of mean kinetic energy into turbulent kinetic energy is
\[
P_k=-\langle u'v'\rangle\frac{\mathrm dU}{\mathrm dy}.
\]
Typically \(\mathrm dU/\mathrm dy>0\) and \(\langle u'v'\rangle<0\), giving positive production. Nonlinear interactions transfer energy between scales, and viscosity ultimately dissipates it. The original channel DNS studies document these statistics and structures [1, 2].






ImportantWhat supplies the energy?



Pressure forcing supplies mechanical energy to the flow. Mean shear transfers some of it into turbulent fluctuations. The stationary walls impose no-slip and shape the shear, but they do no mechanical work because their velocity is zero. Periodic boundaries do not supply energy either.

title: Tutorial 3: Turbulent channel flow
section: 3 How would we run the simulation?
text:
3 How would we run the simulation?
A standard fully developed channel calculation uses a finite domain of dimensions \(L_x\times2\delta\times L_z\):

Impose no-slip and no-penetration at both walls.
Impose periodic velocity boundary conditions in \(x\) and \(z\). Fluid leaving one periodic face re-enters through the opposite face.
Drive the streamwise flow with a mean pressure gradient or its equivalent uniform acceleration.
Initialize turbulence, run through the transient, and monitor bulk velocity, wall stress and kinetic energy.
Once the statistics no longer drift systematically, accumulate averages over many flow time scales. Check their convergence using separate averaging intervals.

With a prescribed pressure gradient, define
\[
g=-\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\mathrm d\overline p}{\mathrm dx}>0.
\]
The streamwise momentum equation contains the acceleration \(g\). Equivalently, split pressure into a linear driving part and a periodic remainder: \(p=-\rho gx+\widetilde p\). Use one representation of the forcing, not both. At statistical equilibrium,
\[
\tau_w=\rho g\delta.
\]
Alternatively, prescribe the bulk velocity
\[
U_b=\frac{1}{2\delta}\int_0^{2\delta}U(y)\,\mathrm dy
\]
and adjust the forcing to maintain it. For fixed pressure gradient the flow rate responds; for fixed flow rate the pressure gradient responds. Specify which is controlled when comparing calculations.
DNS solves the unsteady Navier–Stokes equations without a turbulence closure. It needs sufficient spatial and temporal resolution, especially near the walls, and a domain large enough for the relevant motions. Turning off a turbulence model on a coarse grid does not make a calculation a resolved DNS. The original studies describe their numerical methods and resolution choices [1–3]. For this assignment, we analyze their supplied statistics rather than rerun the simulations.

title: Tutorial 3: Turbulent channel flow
text:
4 Running it in non-dimensional form
Normalize all lengths by the channel half-height \(\delta\). The domain is then 2 units tall (walls at \(y=0\) and \(y=2\), centerline at \(y=1\)), and we fix \(\rho=1\) and the kinematic viscosity \(\nu=1\) once and for all. With \(\delta=1\) and \(\nu=1\) the friction Reynolds number collapses to
\[
Re_\tau=\frac{u_\tau\delta}{\nu}=u_\tau ,
\]
so the only thing that distinguishes one Reynolds number from another is the forcing.
\(Re_\tau\) goes into the forcing. A fully developed channel is sustained by a constant streamwise body force \(g\) (a mean pressure gradient). At equilibrium the force over the half-height balances the wall stress,
\[
\tau_w=\rho\,g\,\delta
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
u_\tau=\sqrt{g\,\delta}=\sqrt{g}.
\]
Since we want \(u_\tau=Re_\tau\), set the body force to
\[
g=Re_\tau^{2}.
\]
That is the whole recipe: keep the geometry (height 2) and \(\nu=1\) fixed, and change only the forcing, \(g=Re_\tau^2\), to select the Reynolds number. The non-dimensional momentum equation is
\[
\frac{\partial u_i}{\partial t}+u_j\frac{\partial u_i}{\partial x_j}
=-\frac{\partial \widetilde p}{\partial x_i}
+\frac{\partial^2 u_i}{\partial x_j\,\partial x_j}
+Re_\tau^{2}\,\delta_{i1},
\]
with the single parameter \(Re_\tau\) now living in the forcing term.
Recovering wall units afterwards is immediate: \(u_\tau=Re_\tau\), so \(U^+=U/Re_\tau\) and \(y^+=Re_\tau\,(y/\delta)\).






TipRecipe: one geometry, one \(\nu\), change the forcing




Channel height \(2\) (\(\delta=1\)); a typical domain is \(2\pi\times 2\times \pi\) in \((x,y,z)\).
\(\nu=1\) and \(\rho=1\), the same for every case.
Constant streamwise body force \(g=Re_\tau^{2}\) (e.g. \(395^2\approx1.56\times10^{5}\) for \(Re_\tau=395\)).
Outputs are in viscous units: divide velocities by \(Re_\tau\) to get \(U^+\), and \(y^+=Re_\tau\,(y/\delta)\).
The near-wall spacing in wall units is \(\Delta y^+=Re_\tau\,\Delta y\), so refine the mesh as \(Re_\tau\) grows.



In OpenFOAM the viscosity goes in constant/transportProperties and the constant force is a momentum source in system/fvOptions:


constant/transportProperties

transportModel  Newtonian;
nu              1;        // fixed for every Re_tau



system/fvOptions

momentumSource
{
    type            vectorSemiImplicitSource;   // constant body force = fixed pressure gradient
    selectionMode   all;
    volumeMode      specific;
    injectionRateSuSp
    {
        U   ((156025 0 0) 0);   // g = Re_tau^2,  here Re_tau = 395  ->  395^2 = 156025
    }
}

(The exact fvOptions keyword can vary slightly between OpenFOAM versions; the physics is just a constant source \(Su=(Re_\tau^2,0,0)\) added to every cell.)






NoteFixed force vs. fixed flow rate



Driving with this constant force fixes the wall stress, so you set \(Re_\tau\) directly (through \(g=Re_\tau^2\)) and the bulk velocity \(U_b\) comes out as a result. OpenFOAM’s meanVelocityForce does the opposite: it holds a prescribed bulk velocity and lets the pressure gradient, and therefore \(u_\tau\) and \(Re_\tau\), be the output. Both are valid; just state which one you controlled, and check at equilibrium that the measured \(u_\tau\) (from the wall shear) matches your target.

title: Tutorial 3: Turbulent channel flow
text:
5 From instantaneous fields to statistics
At each wall distance, average over the homogeneous \(x,z\) plane and over time after the transient. Conceptually,
\[
\langle f\rangle(y)=\frac{1}{T L_xL_z}
\int_{t_0}^{t_0+T}\int_0^{L_z}\int_0^{L_x}
f(x,y,z,t)\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dz\,\mathrm dt.
\]
The finite average estimates the statistical mean; correlated samples are not independent realizations. Do not average over \(y\): that would erase the wall-normal variation we want to study.
Define \(U_i=\langle u_i\rangle\) and \(u_i'=u_i-U_i\). Ideally the mean velocity has only one nonzero component, \(U_1=U(y)\).








Quantity
Definition
Interpretation




Mean velocity
\(U(y)=\langle u_1\rangle\)
Average streamwise motion


Normal covariance
\(R_{ii}=\langle (u_i')^2\rangle\), no sum
Variance of one velocity component


RMS fluctuation
\(\sqrt{R_{ii}}\), no sum
Typical fluctuation amplitude, with velocity units


Shear covariance
\(R_{12}=\langle u'v'\rangle\)
Correlated streamwise and wall-normal motion


Turbulent kinetic energy
\(k=(R_{11}+R_{22}+R_{33})/2\)
Fluctuation energy per unit mass


Production
\(P_k=-R_{12}\,\mathrm dU/\mathrm dy\)
Transfer from mean-flow energy into turbulence



The turbulent contribution to mean shear stress is \(-\rho R_{12}\); the tabulated covariance itself has units of velocity squared before normalization. The three normal variances need not be equal.
“Statistically stationary” means that the statistical distribution does not change with time. “Fully developed” means that the mean statistics do not change downstream. Neither means that the instantaneous velocity is steady.

title: Tutorial 3: Turbulent channel flow
text:
6 Wall units and useful checks
Define friction velocity, wall distance and friction Reynolds number by
\[
u_\tau=\sqrt{\tau_w/\rho},\qquad
y^+=\frac{yu_\tau}{\nu},\qquad
U^+=\frac{U}{u_\tau},\qquad
Re_\tau=\frac{u_\tau\delta}{\nu}.
\]
Also \(R_{ij}^+=R_{ij}/u_\tau^2\) and \(P_k^+=\nu P_k/u_\tau^4\). These use wall stress and viscosity to compare different flows. Nondimensionalization is always possible; exact collapse of profiles is an additional physical claim.
Very near a smooth wall, \(U^+\simeq y^+\). This is an asymptotic result. An extended logarithmic region requires sufficient separation between the viscous and outer scales; it should not be assumed throughout the channel.
The same mean momentum equation yields an exact relation for stationary, fully developed flow: the viscous and turbulent shear add up to a total shear that falls off linearly with wall distance, reaching zero at the centerline by symmetry. At the wall, fluctuations vanish and viscosity carries all of the shear; away from it, turbulent transport takes over.






NoteLeft to the assignment



Deriving this total-stress balance, plotting the viscous shear, turbulent shear and their sum, and checking their residual against the exact linear profile are part of Question 1 of Assignment 3, so the derivation and those plots are not reproduced here. Finite sampled DNS statistics can leave a small residual even though the relation is exact.

text:
7 The data used in Assignment 3
Our files come from Moser, Kim and Mansour (1999), with nominal \(Re_\tau=180,395,590\) [2]. Use the actual header values, \(178.12\), \(392.24\) and \(587.19\), in calculations. The official database provides profiles and additional statistics.
The data are available on the cluster at:
/project/60004/02_Assignment3/00_Data/chandata
This directory contains chan180, chan395 and chan590.

TipThree conventions to check before plotting




The files are already normalized. Do not divide their velocities or stresses by \(u_\tau\) again.
The fourth .means column is \(\mathrm dU^+/\mathrm d(y/\delta)\), not \(\mathrm dU^+/\mathrm dy^+\). Working out how the two are related, and applying it, is part of Assignment 3 (Q1).
.reystress contains variances and covariances, not RMS velocities. Read the header of every file, including the signs used for budget terms.




7.1 Starter: reading the ASCII files
The files are plain ASCII: a comment header (lines starting with %) followed by numeric columns. A minimal reader, which you can drop into your notebook and build on:
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np

# On the cluster the data live at the path shown above. For a reproducible submission,
# copy or symlink them next to your notebook and use a RELATIVE path here.
DATA = Path("chandata")      # e.g. ./chandata/chan395/profiles/chan395.means

def peek_header(path, n=12):
    """Print the comment header so you can confirm Re_tau and the column order."""
    for line in Path(path).read_text().splitlines()[:n]:
        if line.lstrip().startswith(("%", "#")):
            print(line)

def load_case(case):
    """Read one case, e.g. load_case('chan395').
    Columns follow the table above; always check the header first with peek_header().
    If loadtxt trips on the header, adjust `comments` or pass skiprows=N."""
    d = DATA / case
    means = np.loadtxt(d / "profiles" / f"{case}.means",     comments=("%", "#"))
    rey   = np.loadtxt(d / "profiles" / f"{case}.reystress", comments=("%", "#"))
    kbal  = np.loadtxt(d / "balances" / f"{case}.kbal",      comments=("%", "#"))
    return {
        "y_delta": means[:, 0], "yplus": means[:, 1], "Uplus": means[:, 2],
        "dUp_dyouter": means[:, 3],       # dU+/d(y/delta), NOT dU+/dy+ (see Assignment 3, Q1)
        "R11": rey[:, 2], "R22": rey[:, 3], "R33": rey[:, 4],
        "R12": rey[:, 5], "R13": rey[:, 6], "R23": rey[:, 7],
        "production": kbal[:, 3],         # production term (see header for normalization/sign)
    }

cases = {name: load_case(name) for name in ("chan180", "chan395", "chan590")}

# sanity check
peek_header(DATA / "chan395" / "profiles" / "chan395.means")
print(cases["chan395"]["Uplus"].shape)
Read \(Re_\tau\) from each file’s header (not the folder name), and keep in mind that the fourth .means column is \(\mathrm dU^+/\mathrm d(y/\delta)\), not \(\mathrm dU^+/\mathrm dy^+\).
The historical sequence is worth distinguishing: Kim, Moin and Moser (1987) established the classic low-Reynolds-number channel study; Moser, Kim and Mansour (1999) supplied the three cases used here; Lee and Moser (2015) extended the investigation to \(Re_\tau\approx5200\), allowing a much wider separation of scales [1–3].
Before starting the assignment, make sure you can answer these.






ImportantSelf-check 1 — What supplies the energy?



The walls are stationary and the streamwise and spanwise boundaries are periodic. Where does the energy that sustains the turbulence come from?








NoteAnswer





The imposed mean pressure gradient (the forcing) does work on the flow and supplies the mechanical energy; mean shear then transfers part of it into the fluctuations (\(P_k=-\langle u'v'\rangle\,\mathrm dU/\mathrm dy\)). The walls do no work because their velocity is zero, and periodic boundaries supply none.









ImportantSelf-check 2 — Why do smooth, \(y\)-only profiles emerge?



The instantaneous field varies in all three directions and in time. Why do the mean statistics depend on \(y\) alone?








NoteAnswer





The flow is statistically stationary and homogeneous in \(x\) and \(z\). Averaging over those two homogeneous directions and over time cancels the three-dimensional, unsteady fluctuations and leaves means that vary only with wall distance \(y\). The instantaneous field stays fully 3-D and unsteady; it is the averaging over the symmetry directions that produces the smooth profiles.









ImportantSelf-check 3 — Zero turbulent shear at a wall with nonzero wall stress?



The wall shear stress \(\tau_w\) is finite, yet the turbulent (Reynolds) shear stress vanishes at the wall. How do these coexist?








NoteAnswer





No-slip forces every fluctuation to vanish at the wall, so \(-\rho\langle u'v'\rangle\to0\) there. The wall stress is carried entirely by the viscous (mean) stress, \(\tau_w=\rho\,\nu\,\mathrm
dU/\mathrm dy\) at \(y=0\), which is finite. Turbulent transport only takes over away from the wall, where the fluctuations grow.

title: Assignment 1 · Part B: The turbulent kinetic energy budget
text:
1 What you will do
In the data-processing tutorial you learned to read the field and manipulate it. Here you use it to evaluate the two central quantities of any turbulence calculation — the turbulent kinetic energy \(k\) and its dissipation rate \(\varepsilon\) — directly from the DNS, and then build the characteristic scales of the flow from them. This mirrors the \(k\)-equation analysis from lecture: instead of modelling these terms, you measure them.

title: Assignment 1 · Part B: The turbulent kinetic energy budget
text:
2 The turbulent kinetic energy equation
Applying the Reynolds decomposition \(u_i = \langle u_i\rangle + u_i'\) to the Navier–Stokes equations and taking the mean gives the transport equation for the turbulent kinetic energy \(k = \tfrac12\langle u_i' u_i'\rangle\):
\[
\underbrace{\frac{\partial k}{\partial t}}_{\text{unsteady}}
+ \underbrace{\langle u_j\rangle \frac{\partial k}{\partial x_j}}_{\text{advection}}
= \underbrace{-\langle u_i' u_j'\rangle \frac{\partial \langle u_i\rangle}{\partial x_j}}_{\text{production } \mathcal{P}}
- \underbrace{\varepsilon}_{\text{dissipation}}
+ \underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}\!\left(\cdots\right)}_{\text{transport } \mathcal{T}}
\tag{1}\]
with the dissipation rate
\[
\varepsilon = 2\nu \langle s_{ij}' s_{ij}'\rangle,
\qquad
s_{ij}' = \tfrac12\!\left(\frac{\partial u_i'}{\partial x_j} + \frac{\partial u_j'}{\partial x_i}\right).
\tag{2}\]






TipWhy the budget collapses for our flow



Forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence is the cleanest possible case for Eq. 1, because almost every term drops out:

No mean shear. \(\langle u_i\rangle \approx 0\) everywhere, so the mean advection term and the production term \(\mathcal{P} = -\langle u_i' u_j'\rangle\,\partial_j\langle u_i\rangle\) both vanish — there is no mean gradient to extract energy from.
Homogeneity. Statistics do not depend on position, so every spatial divergence — the transport term \(\mathcal{T}\) — averages to zero.
Stationarity. The forcing injects energy at the large scales at a mean rate \(\mathcal{F}\) that, on average, holds \(\partial k/\partial t = 0\).

What remains is a single statement: injection balances dissipation, \(\mathcal{F} = \varepsilon\). You cannot measure the artificial forcing \(\mathcal{F}\) from a snapshot, but you can measure \(k\) and \(\varepsilon\) directly — and from them every characteristic scale of the flow. That is the task.

3 Reading the field as a structured cube
The tasks below assume the field has been reshaped from the flat table into a \(200^3\) NumPy array per velocity component. The grid spacing is that of the parent \(1024^3\) simulation, \(dx = 2\pi/1024\), so the sub-cube has side \(L = 200\,dx = 2\pi\,(200/1024)\).

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

nu = 1.85e-4                       # kinematic viscosity of the JHTDB isotropic DNS
dx = 2 * np.pi / 1024              # grid spacing of the parent 1024^3 simulation
dim = 200                          # our sub-cube is 200^3

df = pd.read_parquet("/project/60004/00_Assignment1/isotropic_t1.parquet")  # FULL 200^3 grid at one instant (isotropic.parquet is the time-series, wrong for spatial stats)

def to_cube(component):
    """Scatter a flat velocity column onto the structured 200^3 grid."""
    cube = np.zeros((dim, dim, dim), dtype=np.float64)
    ix = (df["x"] / dx).round().astype(int)
    iy = (df["y"] / dx).round().astype(int)
    iz = (df["z"] / dx).round().astype(int)
    cube[ix, iy, iz] = df[component].values
    return cube

u = to_cube("velocity_x")
v = to_cube("velocity_y")
w = to_cube("velocity_z")
print(u.shape, u.dtype)

Prefer logging over scattered print calls: you get severity levels (DEBUG/INFO/WARNING/ERROR), timestamps, and the ability to turn detail up or down without deleting code.

title: Efficient scientific plotting
text: This tutorial covers best practices and example code for creating high-quality figures directly in Python. The guidelines are based on personal experience — think of them as a set of golden rules that have proven their worth over time. Following them from the start will save you a lot of reformatting work later.

title: Efficient scientific plotting
text:
1 Guidelines for scientific figures
Before diving into code, it is worth establishing a few ground rules for what makes a good scientific figure. Getting these right from the start saves significant rework later.

General plotting style

Consistent style — colour scheme, axis labels, line widths, …
Typeface and font size

LaTeX rendering (optional, for a perfect match).
Match the document by matching font size, figure size, and (optionally) typeface. The recommended figure and font sizes are usually in the journal’s author guidelines.
If created this way, include the figure without scaling in LaTeX — use scale=1 instead of the common width=\textwidth.

Figure quality and resolution

.pdf — line plots and small plots (scalable vector graphics).
.png / .jpeg — colour maps / contour plots (when PDF is impractical, and to avoid silent rescaling).
Sufficient resolution (~1000 dpi, or at least the journal guideline).

Labels and units

Consistent use; units set non-italic (upright).
Typical formatting of a quantity \(T\) in kelvin:

\(T\) / K — recommended by the SI guidelines
\(T\) in K
\(T\) (K)
\(T\) [K]


Data visualization

Unambiguous data representation (e.g. scatter vs. hexbin — see below).
A high level of self-explanation — readers often skim a paper looking only at the figures.

title: Efficient scientific plotting
text:
2 Defining a consistent plotting style
A key aspect of high-quality figures is a consistent design across all of them: font size, typeface, text rendering, colour scheme, axis design, and so on. Below we build up from the approach most beginners reach for to the one worth adopting — Matplotlib stylesheets.
Our target style: a colour-blind-friendly colour cycle (the tableau 10-blind palette) paired with a set of line styles (why colour-blind-friendly?).

import matplotlib as mpl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

tableau10blind = [
    "#006BA4", "#FF800E", "#ABABAB", "#595959", "#5F9ED1",
    "#C85200", "#898989", "#A2C8EC", "#FFBC79", "#CFCFCF",
]
linestyles = ["-", "--", "-.", ":", "-", "--", "-.", ":", "-", "--"]


2.1 Approach 1 — style inside each command (beginner)
The most intuitive approach: set every option directly in the plotting calls.



Pros
Cons




Intuitive
Tedious — repeat it for every axis and figure


Simple to understand
Inefficient; clutters the code




fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for i in range(4):
    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, i + 1], color=tableau10blind[i],
            linestyle=linestyles[i])
ax.set_xlabel("$x$ (m)", fontsize=16)
ax.set_ylabel("$y$ (m)", fontsize=16)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=16)
ax.legend([f"$\\Phi={i}$" for i in range(4)], fontsize=16)
plt.show()










2.2 Approach 2 — Matplotlib rcParams (intermediate)
rcParams let you set styles once; they then apply to every plot below the definition.



Pros
Cons




Central definition, more efficient
Still lives in each script


No per-command repetition
Leads to code duplication across files




plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.size": 16,
    "font.family": "serif",
    "mathtext.fontset": "cm",   # Computer-Modern math without a LaTeX install
    "axes.prop_cycle": mpl.cycler(color=tableau10blind, linestyle=linestyles),
})

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for i in range(4):
    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, i + 1])
ax.set_xlabel("$x$ (m)")
ax.set_ylabel("$y$ (m)")
ax.legend([f"$\\Phi={i}$" for i in range(4)])
plt.show()
plt.rcdefaults()   # reset for the next section










2.3 Approach 3 — Matplotlib stylesheets (recommended)
The gold standard is a stylesheet — a small .mplstyle file holding your defaults.
Pros: central definition, easy reuse across projects, highly flexible, and very clean code — with essentially no downside.
A stylesheet is a plain-text list of key : value settings. A good starting style (save it as mystyle.mplstyle):
figure.figsize   : 6.0, 4.0     # inches
figure.dpi       : 120          # on-screen scaling
savefig.dpi      : 500          # dpi when saving raster output
xtick.direction  : in
ytick.direction  : in
legend.frameon   : False
font.family      : serif
mathtext.fontset : cm
font.size        : 14
image.cmap       : turbo
# colour-blind-friendly colour + line-style cycle
axes.prop_cycle  : (cycler('color', ['006BA4','FF800E','ABABAB','595959','5F9ED1','C85200','898989','A2C8EC','FFBC79','CFCFCF']) + cycler('linestyle', ['-','--','-.',':','-','--','-.',':','-','--']))
Apply it with plt.style.use('mystyle.mplstyle'). The three files used in this course — mystyle (base), mcgill-colors, and PROCI (journal, LaTeX) — are provided in the plotting-styles/ folder next to this notebook. Below we load the base style from a temporary file so the example is self-contained.

import tempfile, pathlib

MYSTYLE = '''
figure.figsize   : 6.0, 4.0
figure.dpi       : 120
savefig.dpi      : 500
xtick.direction  : in
ytick.direction  : in
legend.frameon   : False
font.family      : serif
mathtext.fontset : cm
font.size        : 14
image.cmap       : turbo
axes.prop_cycle  : (cycler('color', ['006BA4','FF800E','ABABAB','595959','5F9ED1','C85200','898989','A2C8EC','FFBC79','CFCFCF']) + cycler('linestyle', ['-','--','-.',':','-','--','-.',':','-','--']))
'''

style_dir = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(style_dir / "mystyle.mplstyle").write_text(MYSTYLE)

plt.rcdefaults()
plt.style.use(str(style_dir / "mystyle.mplstyle"))

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for i in range(4):
    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, i + 1])
ax.set_xlabel("$x$ (m)")
ax.set_ylabel("$y$ (m)")
ax.legend([f"$\\Phi={i}$" for i in range(4)])
plt.show()









2.3.1 Make styles globally available
Place your .mplstyle files in Matplotlib’s config directory and they become available in every script — no path needed, just plt.style.use('mystyle').

print("put your styles here:", mpl.get_configdir() + "/stylelib")
print("some built-in styles:", plt.style.available[:8])

put your styles here: /root/.config/matplotlib/stylelib
some built-in styles: ['Solarize_Light2', '_classic_test_patch', '_mpl-gallery', '_mpl-gallery-nogrid', 'bmh', 'classic', 'dark_background', 'fast']




2.3.2 Combine styles, and apply one locally
Styles compose: a base style plus a journal/medium-specific one (font and figure size for a paper vs. a poster). You can also apply a style to a single figure with a with context, leaving everything else untouched.

POSTER = 'font.size: 20\nlines.linewidth: 3\n'
MCGILL = ("axes.prop_cycle: cycler('color', "
          "['ED1B2F','F7941D','27B0BE','305534','024F6D','B2D235'])\n")
(style_dir / "poster.mplstyle").write_text(POSTER)
(style_dir / "mcgill.mplstyle").write_text(MCGILL)

def demo(ax):
    for i in range(3):
        ax.plot([0, 1], [0, i + 1])
    ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$y$")

# base + poster overrides, combined in a list (later wins)
plt.rcdefaults()
plt.style.use([str(style_dir / "mystyle.mplstyle"),
               str(style_dir / "poster.mplstyle")])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 2.6)); demo(ax)
ax.set_title("base + poster"); plt.show()

# McGill colours for THIS figure only
with plt.style.context([str(style_dir / "mystyle.mplstyle"),
                        str(style_dir / "mcgill.mplstyle")]):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 2.6)); demo(ax)
    ax.set_title("McGill colours (local)"); plt.show()
plt.rcdefaults()

















2.3.3 Make it fail-safe
If a style might not be installed on every machine, guard it so your script still runs:
try:
    plt.style.use(['mystyle', 'PROCI'])
except OSError:
    print("Matplotlib styles not found — using defaults")


2.3.4 For a journal: true LaTeX rendering
For a perfect typeface match, a journal style enables LaTeX typesetting. This needs a working LaTeX toolchain (and the right fonts/packages), so the PROCI.mplstyle below is shown for reference and not executed here:
font.family         : serif
font.serif          : Times New Roman
text.usetex         : true
font.size           : 7
text.latex.preamble : \usepackage{amsmath}\usepackage{times}
lines.linewidth     : 1.0
savefig.bbox        : tight
Imagine you need to relabel the temperature axis across 15 figures from T (K) to T / K. Hand-typing LaTeX 15 times invites typos — a label dictionary keeps one source of truth. This is super easy in Python using a dict with .get() fallbacks.

Efficient scientific plotting
text:
4 Figure size and file format
Draw the figure at the width it will occupy (one column ≈ 3.5 in) and place it in LaTeX with scale=1. Save line plots as .pdf (vector, sharp at any zoom) and colour maps / contour plots as .png at high dpi (a vector version would be huge).

GOLDEN = (1 + 5 ** 0.5) / 2
x = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 400)

plt.rcdefaults()
plt.rcParams.update({"font.family": "serif", "mathtext.fontset": "cm",
                     "font.size": 9})
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3.5, 3.5 / GOLDEN))
ax.plot(x, np.sin(x), label=r"$\sin(x)$")
ax.set_xlabel(r"$t \; / \; \mathrm{s}$")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$u \; / \; \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.3)
fig.savefig("lineplot.pdf")            # vector, for a line plot
plt.show()








Imagine you need to plot a \(u'\)–\(v'\) cloud of two million points. A scatter plot turns into a solid black blob; you need to show density. This is super easy in Python using hexbin.

title: Efficient scientific plotting
text:
5 Unambiguous data: scatter vs. hexbin
A scatter plot of many points overplots — dense regions saturate and hide the true distribution. For large samples a 2-D density (hexbin) is honest and readable.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 20_000
xd = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
yd = xd * 0.6 + rng.normal(0, 0.6, n)

fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7, 2.6))
a1.scatter(xd, yd, s=4, alpha=0.3, edgecolors="none")
a1.set_title("scatter (overplotted)")
hb = a2.hexbin(xd, yd, gridsize=40, cmap="viridis", mincnt=1)
a2.set_title("hexbin (density)")
fig.colorbar(hb, ax=a2, label="count")
for a in (a1, a2):
    a.set_xlabel(r"$x$"); a.set_ylabel(r"$y$")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.4)
plt.show()
